evidence: G-S31. I judged the draft "You may have fooled yourself in the past, and that part remembers." in the second paragraph of the section "It feels fake", against his words it replaces ("Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers.") and the inner child guide passage in SOURCE.txt. Does what the_change says: Emulate's opener "You may have fooled yourself in the past" followed by his own "and that part remembers". CONTEXT.txt holds it once, as in DRAFT.txt, and his next sentence ("Tell me what you remember, I'm listening." works well here.) stands after it unchanged, word for word as in SOURCE.txt. (The same CONTEXT.txt also carries the neighbouring change in the first paragraph; I read the section with both in and the two do not touch.) Meaning: the same hedged possibility that the reader has fooled themselves before ("Maybe you've ... before" becomes "You may have ... in the past") and the same remembering part, with his "remembers" kept and the lead-in to his quoted line ("Tell me what you remember") intact. No claim or fact is added. The hedge now sits on "may have" in the first clause, and "and that part remembers" follows as it did after "Maybe" in his sentence; an ordinary reader gets the same "if you did, that part remembers". It reads a notch more formal than his "Maybe you've ... before", but inside this paragraph's modal register ("You could say", "there could be something to it") and beside his casual lines ("that one can sting", "works well here"). Reads right in context: it follows the sentence before it ("If it says yes, that one can sting, because there could be something to it.") by saying what the something might be, and it ties back to the part's own question "Are you afraid I will lie to myself again?", whose "again" is the earlier fooling. Pronouns: "that part" is the protecting part the section introduces ("a part that is protecting you") and the paragraph is addressing ("If it says yes"), exactly as in his sentence; "yourself" is the reader. Tell rows: none PRESENT. The closest is T15: the opener is a straight rewording of his ("Maybe" / "you've" / "before" becomes "You may have" / "in the past") with the structure and his tail kept. I judge it not present: the swap goes to plainer, more common phrasing, not to rarer words; his sentence has no other tell for a swap to hide; and it is the humanizing tool's own opener, not the thesaurus substitution T15 describes. Also weighed: T21 (two coordinated clauses, but one thought, why the sting is fair, not two argumentative jobs), T22 (it gives a reason the part's fear may be fair and says the part remembers; it does not just reassure), T26 ("remember" / "remembers" and "part" repeat, but as the callback his quoted line is built on), T20 ("and that part remembers" is his own mid-paragraph clause, not a closer), T23 and T06 (no scenery, and "part" is the article's own term), T13/T09/T14 (one clause replaced where it stood; nothing moved or added), C02/C03/C04 (referents land, no first-person fact, no outside claim). Linter: "D9 follows the source order" accepted, because it is one clause replaced where it stood, so agreement 1.00 is automatic, and T13/T09 are answered as above. "E36/E41 heavy second person" accepted: 8.3 per 100 is one "you" in a 12-word sentence (his sentence had one in 9 words, about 11 per 100 if "you've" counts, so this is lighter), the guide speaks to the reader as "you" throughout, and the sentence gives a reason, not coach reassurance.
